questions.question: What is the best first step before ordering a diagnostic test?
choices: Order the broadest available panel
Define the clinical question and how the result could change management
Select the most expensive study
Wait until the differential contains only one diagnosis
questions.explanation: Testing should answer a defined screening, diagnostic, severity, monitoring, or prognostic question and have a planned consequence.

questions.question: Why can a positive test have a low positive predictive value in a very low-risk population?
choices: Sensitivity becomes zero
Specificity is irrelevant
False-positive results may outnumber true positives when disease prevalence is very low
Reference intervals disappear
questions.explanation: Predictive value depends on disease prevalence and pretest probability, so low-risk testing can produce a high proportion of false positives.

questions.question: A patient with CKD and weakness has potassium 6.8 mEq/L from a hemolyzed specimen. What is the safest response?
choices: Assume pseudohyperkalemia and repeat next month
Stop all evaluation because hemolysis proves the value is false
Immediately assess the patient, obtain ECG and urgent reliable repeat testing, and treat or transfer if confirmed or electrically toxic
Advise dietary change only
questions.explanation: Hemolysis can elevate potassium falsely, but symptoms and CKD create high risk. Verification must occur urgently without delaying management of true hyperkalemia.

questions.question: Which approach is most appropriate for evaluating anemia?
choices: Prescribe iron for every low hemoglobin
Classify by indices, assess reticulocyte response, and integrate bleeding, nutrition, kidney disease, inflammation, medications, and other causes
Use the white-cell count alone
Ignore the trend if the patient is ambulatory
questions.explanation: Anemia is a syndrome. MCV, reticulocyte response, history, related studies, and clinical context guide the differential and treatment.

questions.question: A patient has anemia with recent blood loss, repeatedly elevated fasting plasma glucose, and a less elevated A1C. What is the best interpretation?
choices: A1C always overrides plasma glucose
Red-cell turnover may distort A1C, so appropriate plasma glucose criteria and confirmation should be used
Diabetes is impossible when tests disagree
No follow-up is needed
questions.explanation: Conditions affecting red-cell turnover can make A1C unreliable. Significant discordance requires investigation and use of appropriate plasma glucose criteria.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects KDIGO's approach to chronic kidney disease?
choices: One elevated creatinine during dehydration proves CKD
CKD requires a urine culture
CKD is based on kidney abnormalities present for at least three months and is classified by cause, GFR, and albuminuria
Serum creatinine alone fully defines kidney risk
questions.explanation: Chronicity matters, and KDIGO uses cause, GFR category, and albuminuria category because creatinine alone is incomplete.

questions.question: A patient has a positive urine culture but no urinary symptoms. What is the best general principle?
choices: Treat every positive culture
Interpret symptoms, collection quality, host, and indications because asymptomatic bacteriuria is not treated routinely outside defined exceptions
Repeat antibiotics until the culture is sterile
Ignore pregnancy status
questions.explanation: Culture positivity can reflect asymptomatic bacteriuria or contamination. Pregnancy and selected urologic procedures are important exceptions under current guidance.

questions.question: What does an elevated troponin establish by itself?
choices: Type 1 myocardial infarction in every patient
Myocardial injury that requires clinical, ECG, timing, serial, and etiologic interpretation
Normal coronary arteries
A diagnosis of heart failure only
questions.explanation: Troponin indicates myocardial injury, but the cause and whether myocardial infarction criteria are met require clinical context and serial interpretation.

questions.question: Which is an example of a preanalytic laboratory error?
choices: Failure to call the patient about a result
Incorrect interpretation of a likelihood ratio
Hemolysis or mislabeling before the specimen is measured
Failure to arrange referral after imaging
questions.explanation: Preanalytic errors occur before measurement and include patient identification, collection, labeling, transport, timing, and specimen-quality problems.

questions.question: What best defines closed-loop test-result management?
choices: Releasing the result to a portal only
Assuming another clinician will review it
Ensuring the result is received, acknowledged, communicated understandably, acted upon, and tracked to completion
Documenting the order but not the outcome
questions.explanation: Closed-loop management extends from ordering and specimen completion through review, communication, action, and verification that follow-up occurred.
